overview.title: LSTM results and the idea of memory in RNNs
overview.main_topic: Figure 13.5 (LSTM training/validation MAE) and the conceptual introduction of recurrent networks: feedforward networks have no memory, while RNNs iterate over a sequence and maintain a state
overview.central_idea: Dense networks and ConvNets are feedforward. They process each input independently, so a sequence must be shown all at once as a single data point. An RNN instead loops over the sequence elements while keeping a state that summarizes what it has seen, a highly simplified version of how people read.
overview.importance: This page moves from 'the LSTM works' to 'why it works'. The concepts of state and internal loop introduced here underlie everything that follows: the toy RNN in NumPy (p.390), SimpleRNN, LSTM and GRU in Keras (p.392ff.).
learning_objectives: Read Figure 13.5: best validation MAE around epoch 4–5, and the onset of overfitting afterwards.
Explain why epoch 1 is omitted from the plot.
Define a feedforward network and explain why it has 'no memory'.
Describe how an RNN processes a sequence: iterate over elements, maintain a state, internal loop.
Relate the dense model of p.384 (flattening five days into one vector) to the feedforward paradigm.

summary:
**Figure 13.5** shows training and validation MAE of the LSTM model from Listing 13.12. Epoch 1 is omitted because its training MAE of **7.75** would distort the scale. From epoch 2 to 10, training MAE falls steadily from about 2.89 to about 2.27 °C. Validation MAE drops from about 2.58 to a minimum of about **2.40 °C around epochs 4–5**, consistent with the 2.39 reported on p.388 and below the 2.44 °C baseline. It then creeps back up to about 2.47 °C by epoch 10. The curves cross around epoch 5–6, after which the model overfits.

The authors then ask why the LSTM did *markedly better* than the dense model and the ConvNet, and how it can be refined. To answer that, they take a closer look at recurrent networks.

**Section 13.3.1** starts from a property of every network seen so far, dense and convolutional: they have **no memory**. Each input is processed independently, with no state kept between inputs. To process a sequence with such a network, you have to show it the whole sequence at once as a single data point, which is what the dense model did by flattening five days of data into one big vector. These are called **feedforward networks**.

By contrast, when you read a sentence you process it word by word (really, *eye saccade by eye saccade*) while remembering what came before, which gives you a fluid representation of its meaning. Biological intelligence processes information **incrementally**, maintaining an internal model built from past information and updated as new information arrives. A **recurrent neural network (RNN)** adopts the same principle in an *extremely simplified* form. It iterates through the sequence elements while maintaining a **state** that contains information about what it has seen so far. In effect, an RNN is a network with an internal **loop** (Figure 13.6, next page).

paragraphs.what_it_says: The caption describes the training and validation MAE of the LSTM model, and notes that epoch 1 is omitted because its very high training MAE (7.75) would distort the scale.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In the plot (epochs 2–10), validation MAE reaches about 2.40 °C at epochs 4–5 and then rises slowly to about 2.47. paragraphs.excerpt: A major characteristic of all neural networks you’ve seen so far, such
paragraphs.what_it_says: All networks seen so far, dense and convolutional, have no memory: each input is processed independently, with no state kept between inputs. To process a sequence, you must show it whole as a single data point, as the dense model did by flattening five days of data into one vector. Such networks are called feedforward networks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'No memory' means the network's output for one input doesn't depend on any previous input. Information flows strictly forward from input to output in one pass. A feedforward model can still look at a sequence, but only by receiving all of it simultaneously as one big tensor, (120, 14) or 1,680 numbers here. Any relation between timesteps must then be learned from scratch through weights.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It names the limitation that explains the dense model's weakness (p.388: flattening 'removed the notion of time') and sets up the contrast with stateful processing.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A convnet does process local windows, but in parallel with no carried-over state, so it is also feedforward.

terminology.meaning: A network in which data flows in one direction from input to output, with no loops or state carried between inputs.

paragraphs.excerpt: In contrast, as you’re reading the present sentence, you’re processing it word
paragraphs.what_it_says: When you read, you process the sentence word by word (or saccade by saccade) while remembering what came before, which builds a fluid representation of meaning. Biological intelligence processes information incrementally, maintaining an internal model built from the past and constantly updated with new information.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the intuition RNNs are built on. Understanding accumulates: your interpretation of the current word depends on everything earlier, held in a compact running summary rather than by re-reading the whole text.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives an intuitive model of what 'state' means before the formal definition.

terminology.meaning: A rapid jump of the eye between fixation points while reading.
Handling input piece by piece while updating an internal representation.

paragraphs.excerpt: A recurrent neural network (RNN) adopts the same principle, albeit in an
paragraphs.what_it_says: An RNN applies the same principle in an extremely simplified way: it processes a sequence by iterating through its elements while maintaining a state containing information about what it has seen so far. An RNN is a network with an internal loop (Figure 13.6).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of one big computation over 1,680 numbers, the RNN does 120 small steps. Each step takes the current 14-feature vector and the previous state and produces a new state, using the same weights at each step. After the last step, the state summarizes the whole window, with recency built in because later inputs are applied last.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the core definition behind every recurrent layer in the chapter. It explains why the LSTM beat the other models: it reads the data as an ordered sequence.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book on this page: formally $h_t = f(x_t, h_{t-1})$ with shared parameters; p.390 implements this loop in NumPy.

terminology.meaning: Recurrent neural network, a network with an internal loop over sequence elements.
The repeated application of the same step function over timesteps, feeding the state back in.

concepts.name: Feedforward network
concepts.definition: A network without memory: each input is processed independently with no state kept between inputs.
concepts.intuition: A function applied once to a snapshot.
concepts.technical: Output depends only on the current input tensor; sequences must be presented whole, e.g. flattened to a single vector.
concepts.significance: Explains why dense and conv models struggle with order.
concepts.example: The dense model received five days as one 1,680-dimensional vector.
concepts.misconception: That convnets are not feedforward because they slide windows; they still have no state between inputs.

concepts.name: Recurrent neural network
concepts.definition: A network that iterates through sequence elements while maintaining a state containing information about what it has seen so far.
concepts.intuition: Reading word by word while remembering the story.
concepts.technical: A step function with shared weights is applied at each timestep, taking the current input and the previous state; an 'internal loop'.
concepts.significance: The architecture family that finally beats the baseline.
concepts.example: For a (120, 14) window: 120 iterations, each consuming a 14-vector.
concepts.misconception: That an RNN carries memory between different samples; the state is reset between independent sequences (p.390).

concepts.name: State of an RNN
concepts.definition: An internal vector carrying information about the sequence elements processed so far.
concepts.intuition: A running summary or short-term memory.
concepts.technical: Updated at every step; its final value is the default output of Keras recurrent layers.
concepts.significance: Lets the model weigh recent information and keep order.
concepts.example: LSTM(16) has a 16-dimensional output state (plus an internal carry).
concepts.misconception: That the state stores the entire history verbatim; it is a fixed-size, lossy summary.

concepts.name: LSTM training behaviour
concepts.definition: How the LSTM of Listing 13.12 trains on Jena.
concepts.intuition: Starts very badly (epoch-1 training MAE 7.75), learns quickly, then overfits after about 5 epochs.
concepts.technical: Validation MAE minimum ≈ 2.40 near epochs 4–5 in Figure 13.5; reported best 2.39.
concepts.significance: First model below the baseline; overfitting motivates recurrent dropout.
concepts.misconception: That the epoch-10 model is the one evaluated; the checkpoint keeps the best epoch.

deeper.title: Feedforward vs recurrent processing of one Jena window
deeper.body:
**Feedforward (dense model):** one step: $y = f(\text{flatten}(X))$, where $X \in \mathbb{R}^{120\times 14}$. Every weight belongs to a specific (hour, feature) pair.

**Recurrent:** 120 steps: $h_t = g(x_t, h_{t-1})$ for $t = 1..120$, then $y = W h_{120} + b$. The same weights in $g$ are used at every hour, so the model learns *one* rule for 'how a new hour updates my belief' rather than 120 separate rules.

(Formalization beyond the book; the book implements it in NumPy on p.390.)

deeper.title: Reading analogy, made concrete
deeper.body: Imagine reading a weather diary one hour at a time with a small notepad (the state) that has room for only 16 numbers. After each entry you update the notepad. At the end, you forecast tomorrow from the notepad alone. You'd naturally keep recent trends and drop old details, which is what a well-trained LSTM learns to do.

takeaways: Figure 13.5: LSTM validation MAE bottoms out around 2.40 °C (epochs 4–5), below the 2.44 baseline, then rises: overfitting.
Epoch 1 is omitted from the plot because its training MAE (7.75) would distort the scale.
Dense networks and ConvNets are feedforward: no memory, each input processed independently, so a sequence must be one data point.
Humans read incrementally while maintaining an internal model; RNNs copy this in an extremely simplified way.
An RNN iterates over sequence elements, maintains a state and is effectively a network with an internal loop.

questions.question: Why is epoch 1 omitted from Figure 13.5?
questions.answer: Its training MAE was very high (7.75), which would distort the plot's scale.

questions.question: What does the book mean by saying dense networks and ConvNets 'have no memory'?
options: Each input is processed independently with no state kept between inputs
They forget their training after each epoch
questions.answer: Each input is processed independently with no state kept between inputs
questions.explanation: That is the book's definition. Weights are stored and persist across epochs, and ConvNets handle images well.

questions.question: How did the dense model of p.384 handle the sequence, and why does that make it a feedforward approach?
questions.answer: It flattened five days of data into one large vector and processed it in one go, so the whole sequence became a single data point processed in one pass with no state.
questions.explanation: The page uses exactly this example to illustrate feedforward networks.

questions.question: In one sentence, how does an RNN process a sequence according to the page?
questions.answer: It iterates through the sequence elements while maintaining a state containing information about what it has seen so far, an internal loop.
questions.explanation: Direct paraphrase of the RNN definition.

questions.question: Based on Figure 13.5, around which epochs does the LSTM reach its best validation MAE?
questions.explanation: Validation MAE is lowest (≈ 2.40) at epochs 4–5. At epoch 2 it is still about 2.58, and by epochs 8 and 10 it has risen to about 2.43 and 2.47.

questions.question: What does the reading analogy capture about RNNs, and what does 'extremely simplified' warn against?
questions.answer: It captures incremental processing with a continually updated internal summary; 'extremely simplified' warns that an RNN is a crude mechanism, not a model of biological cognition.
questions.explanation: The page draws the analogy and then qualifies it.

questions.question: Could you sketch, with arrows, the difference between how the dense model and an RNN consume a (120, 14) window?
questions.answer: Dense: (120,14) → flatten → one pass. RNN: x_1 → step → h_1, x_2 + h_1 → step → h_2, …, h_120 → output.
questions.explanation: Self-check; compare with Figure 13.6 on p.390.
